question: Which pathogenic mechanism describes anemia caused by inadequate erythrocyte formation?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Hypoproliferative anemia results when the marrow produces an inadequate number of erythrocytes.
This mechanism produces hemolytic anemia and would fit evidence of circulating free hemoglobin.
This mechanism produces hemolysis within macrophage-rich organs and would fit increased splenic sequestration.
This mechanism would require recent hemorrhage rather than inadequate marrow production.
This mechanism would require persistent bleeding and may eventually deplete available iron.

question: Anemia with an MCV below 80 fL belongs to which morphologic category?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Chromicity describes hemoglobinization rather than the MCV category requested.
Normocytic anemia has an MCV within the 80-100 fL interval.
Microcytic anemia is defined by an MCV below 80 fL.
Macrocytic anemia has an MCV above 100 fL.
Hemolytic anemia is a pathogenic category and may have a normal or mildly increased MCV.

question: Which serum protein binds free hemoglobin released during intravascular erythrocyte destruction?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Erythropoietin stimulates marrow erythroid production and would fit a compensatory response to anemia.
Hemoglobin F is an intracellular hemoglobin rather than the serum scavenger of released hemoglobin.
Protoporphyrin participates in heme formation and does not bind circulating free hemoglobin.
ADAMTS13 cleaves large von Willebrand factor multimers and would fit thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Haptoglobin binds circulating free hemoglobin and is consumed when substantial intravascular hemolysis occurs.

question: Which red cell membrane protein is associated with hereditary spherocytosis when structurally abnormal?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: β-Globin abnormalities produce hemoglobinopathies rather than the membrane instability of hereditary spherocytosis.
Spectrin is a membrane cytoskeletal protein whose disruption reduces erythrocyte deformability and promotes splenic destruction.
Carbonic anhydrase supports carbon dioxide transport and is not the implicated membrane scaffold.
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase protects against oxidative injury and would fit episodic oxidant-associated hemolysis.
PIGA is required for glycolipid-linked surface proteins and would fit paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

question: A patient has increased red cell mass and an erythropoietin concentration below the reference interval. Which disorder best accounts for this combination?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Relative polycythemia reflects reduced plasma volume rather than an absolute increase in red cell mass.
Secondary polycythemia is associated with elevated erythropoietin rather than a suppressed concentration.
Polycythemia vera produces an absolute increase in red cell mass with low or normal erythropoietin.
Acute hemorrhage decreases red cell mass and stimulates erythropoietin production.
Aplastic anemia reduces marrow production and would cause anemia rather than erythrocytosis.

question: A marrow specimen is markedly hypercellular in the erythroid lineage, and the peripheral reticulocyte percentage is substantially increased. Which process is best supported?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.text: Effective marrow response to red cell loss
options.rationale: This describes the general response but does not identify the sustained blood-loss process demonstrated by the case pattern.
Maturation failure would not produce the marked circulating reticulocytosis seen here.

options.text: Suppression of all marrow cell lines
options.rationale: Global marrow suppression causes hypocellularity and pancytopenia rather than erythroid hyperplasia.

options.text: Chronic blood loss with marrow compensation
options.rationale: Persistent blood loss can produce erythroid hyperplasia and marked reticulocytosis when iron remains available.
Iron depletion impairs sustained reticulocyte production and would more strongly support microcytic hypochromic cells.

question: An erythrocyte population becomes slightly larger during an appropriate response to anemia. Which cell population produces this MCV change?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Reticulocytes are larger than mature erythrocytes and can mildly increase the measured MCV during marrow compensation.
Spherocytes reflect loss of membrane surface area and would support hereditary or immune-mediated hemolysis.
Schistocytes are fragmented erythrocytes associated with microangiopathic destruction rather than compensatory enlargement.
Target cells are associated with altered hemoglobinization and would fit thalassemia rather than the stated response.
Nucleated erythrocytes with immature leukocytes would support a leukoerythroblastic marrow process.

question: An erythrocyte loses membrane during repeated passage through the spleen but retains its intracellular volume. Which morphologic change is expected?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Sickling results from abnormal hemoglobin polymerization rather than progressive membrane loss.
Fragmentation results from mechanical injury in small vessels rather than splenic membrane removal.
Hypochromia reflects reduced hemoglobin synthesis and would fit iron deficiency or thalassemia.
Basophilic stippling suggests marrow injury from a drug or toxin rather than membrane loss.
Loss of membrane without proportional volume loss produces spherocytes that lack central pallor and have reduced deformability.

question: An immunologic test detects antibodies attached to erythrocytes in a patient with hemolysis. Which mechanism best explains the red cell loss?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: A positive direct antiglobulin test supports immune binding to erythrocytes with subsequent hemolysis.
Oxidative injury would fit glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and would not require attached antibodies.
Microvascular shear produces schistocytes and is not established by an antibody-detection test.
Hereditary membrane instability produces spherocytes but is not mediated by erythrocyte-bound antibodies.
Globin polymerization produces sickling and would fit deoxygenation-associated vaso-occlusion.

question: An erythrocyte membrane loses complement-protective surface proteins because glycolipid anchors cannot be synthesized. Which gene product is defective?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Factor V mutations can promote thrombosis but do not eliminate complement-protective erythrocyte surface proteins.
β-Globin mutations produce hemoglobinopathies rather than loss of glycolipid-anchored proteins.
Spectrin defects reduce erythrocyte deformability and would fit hereditary spherocytosis.
An acquired PIGA mutation prevents expression of glycolipid-anchored complement regulators, causing complement-sensitive blood cells.
A prothrombin mutation may promote thrombosis but does not cause complement-mediated pancytopenic hemolysis.

question: A disorder produces severe anemia despite an expanded erythroid marrow because newly formed globin chains are unbalanced. Which process causes the ineffective erythropoiesis?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Complement-mediated lysis occurs after cells enter the circulation and would fit paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
Autoimmune clearance would be supported by a positive antiglobulin test rather than globin-chain imbalance.
Mechanical fragmentation produces schistocytes and would fit a microangiopathic process.
Oxidative denaturation would fit episodic hemolysis caused by deficient glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.
Unpaired globin chains damage developing erythroid cells, causing intramedullary apoptosis and ineffective erythropoiesis.

question: A patient has reduced plasma volume without an increase in total erythrocyte mass. Which classification best describes the elevated hematocrit?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Secondary polycythemia requires increased red cell mass accompanied by elevated erythropoietin.
Relative polycythemia results from contraction of plasma volume without a true increase in red cell mass.
Primary absolute polycythemia increases red cell mass and is associated with low or normal erythropoietin.
Compensated hemolysis involves increased destruction balanced by production rather than plasma-volume contraction.
Aplastic anemia reflects impaired marrow production and does not explain isolated hemoconcentration.

question: A low oxygen state stimulates an increase in red cell mass. Which laboratory pattern distinguishes this process from polycythemia vera?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Reduced erythropoietin supports autonomous erythrocyte production in polycythemia vera.
A normal concentration may occur in polycythemia vera and does not identify a hypoxia-driven response.
Secondary polycythemia is driven by increased erythropoietin, unlike polycythemia vera.
Absent erythropoietin would oppose the proposed compensatory mechanism.
Depleted haptoglobin supports intravascular hemolysis rather than increased erythrocyte production.

question: Which finding most directly differentiates microangiopathic erythrocyte destruction from splenic destruction of poorly deformable erythrocytes?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Erythroid hyperplasia can accompany either hemolytic process and does not distinguish the site or mechanism.
Reticulocytosis is a compensatory finding shared by both forms of hemolysis.
Low haptoglobin supports free hemoglobin release but is less specific than the characteristic morphology.
Schistocytes indicate mechanical fragmentation in the microvasculature rather than splenic trapping of spherocytes.
Increased precursor production is a general marrow response to accelerated erythrocyte loss.

question: A globin abnormality promotes erythrocyte deformation under reduced oxygen tension. Which downstream event most directly produces painful ischemic episodes?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Deformed erythrocytes adhere within small vessels, obstruct blood flow, and produce ischemic pain.
Splenic sequestration contributes to hemolysis but does not directly explain the painful vascular occlusions.
Baseline disease generally stimulates erythropoiesis; suppression would fit a superimposed aplastic crisis.

options.text: Iron sequestration and reduced heme synthesis
options.rationale: Reduced heme synthesis causes microcytosis rather than deoxygenation-dependent vaso-occlusion.
This mechanism describes immune hemolysis and would be supported by a positive antiglobulin test.

question: A 19-year-old woman undergoes repair of a liver laceration after losing 1 L of blood. Three days later, she remains stable and has adequate iron stores. Which peripheral blood finding is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Basophilic stippling suggests marrow injury from a drug or toxin rather than uncomplicated recovery from hemorrhage.
Hypochromia would require impaired hemoglobin synthesis, as occurs after iron depletion or with thalassemia.
Leukoerythroblastosis suggests marrow infiltration with release of immature myeloid and erythroid cells.
Schistocytes would support microangiopathic fragmentation accompanying shock or sepsis.
Acute blood loss stimulates marrow erythropoiesis, producing a delayed increase in circulating reticulocytes.

question: A 25-year-old woman has a photosensitive facial eruption, arthralgias, pallor, and a positive direct antiglobulin test. Hemoglobin is 8.1 g/dL [12.0-16.0 g/dL], and the reticulocyte percentage is 7% [0.5-2.5%]. Which additional result is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Iron recycling can remain available during hemolysis, but this finding is less directly linked to released plasma hemoglobin.
The marrow is responding appropriately, so reticulocytes are increased rather than decreased.
Hemolysis releases hemoglobin that consumes circulating haptoglobin, lowering its measured concentration.
Hemoglobin F elevation relates to globin composition and is not produced by antibody-mediated hemolysis.
Protoporphyrin elevation would fit impaired heme synthesis rather than immune erythrocyte destruction.

question: A 28-year-old woman has lifelong anemia, splenomegaly, and erythrocytes lacking central pallor. Her affected cells are poorly deformable. Which cellular defect best explains this presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Reduced α-globin production causes a microcytic hemoglobin-synthesis disorder rather than spherical cells.
Reduced β-globin production causes thalassemia with hypochromic microcytes rather than membrane instability.
Defective anchors cause loss of complement-protective proteins and would fit paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
A spectrin-related cytoskeletal defect causes membrane loss, spherocyte formation, and splenic destruction.
An oxidative defense defect produces episodic injury after oxidant exposure rather than persistent spherocytosis.

question: A patient with an inherited membrane cytoskeletal disorder has chronic anemia and splenomegaly. Removal of the spleen improves the anemia. Which change most directly explains this benefit?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Splenectomy prevents poorly deformable spherocytes from being retained and destroyed in splenic cords.
The disorder is caused by a structural membrane defect rather than antibodies directed against erythrocytes.
Splenectomy does not correct the inherited cytoskeletal defect or restore spectrin synthesis.
Iron storage is not the limiting mechanism in this membrane disorder.
The benefit comes from eliminating splenic trapping rather than altering reactive oxygen species production.

question: An 18-year-old woman with hereditary spherocytosis develops fever followed by profound anemia and an extremely low reticulocyte percentage. Serum bilirubin is normal. Which process best explains the acute deterioration?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Accelerated hemolysis would increase bilirubin and provoke reticulocytosis if marrow production remained intact.
Immune hemolysis would increase erythrocyte destruction and would not explain profound reticulocytopenia.
Disseminated coagulation would produce platelet consumption and fragmented erythrocytes rather than isolated production failure.
Temporary shutdown of erythrocyte production causes an aplastic crisis with severe anemia and absent reticulocyte compensation.
Iron deficiency develops more gradually and would produce microcytic hypochromic cells rather than an abrupt crisis.

question: A 3-year-old child has severe hypochromic microcytic anemia, reticulocytosis, maxillary prominence, and expanded marrow spaces. Serum iron is normal. Which mechanism is most likely?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Membrane fragility produces spherocytes and splenic hemolysis rather than profound microcytosis with marrow expansion.
The central defect is imbalance between globin chains rather than isolated reduction of fetal hemoglobin.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a macrocytic megaloblastic pattern rather than severe microcytosis.
Iron sequestration would fit chronic inflammatory disease and would not explain the characteristic marrow expansion.
Thalassemia produces unbalanced globin synthesis, ineffective erythropoiesis, hemolysis, and compensatory marrow expansion.

question: A 13-year-old boy has fever, pulmonary infiltrates, and severe extremity pain. The peripheral smear contains crescent-shaped erythrocytes. Which mechanism most directly produces the painful episode?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Hypoxia promotes sickling but does not itself describe the immediate vascular event causing pain.
Complement sensitivity causes intravascular lysis in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria rather than vaso-occlusion.
Sickled cells adhere within small vessels, producing microvascular occlusion and ischemic pain.
Immune hemolysis would be supported by erythrocyte-bound antibodies rather than crescent-shaped cells.
Basement membrane antibodies do not account for the erythrocyte morphology or vaso-occlusive pain.

question: A 10-year-old child with a predominant abnormal β-globin fraction has recurrent pneumococcal meningitis and no palpable spleen. Which process most directly predisposes to these infections?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Endothelial adhesion contributes to vaso-occlusion but its absence would not explain susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria.
The case identifies loss of splenic function rather than defective hepatic production of complement.
The recurrent infection pattern is linked to functional asplenia rather than demonstrated marrow neutrophil failure.
Repeated splenic infarction causes functional asplenia and impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms.
The presentation does not establish deficient immunoglobulin production as the cause of infection.

question: A patient develops episodic hemolysis after exposure to an oxidant medication. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which cellular deficiency best explains the episodes?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Deficient glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase reduces protection against oxidant injury, producing episodic nonimmune hemolysis.
Spectrin deficiency produces chronic spherocytosis and splenic destruction rather than exposure-dependent episodes.
PIGA deficiency causes complement-sensitive blood cells, dark urine, and possible pancytopenia or thrombosis.
ADAMTS13 deficiency causes platelet microthrombi with thrombocytopenia and fragmented erythrocytes.
A β-globin structural abnormality causes deoxygenation-dependent sickling rather than oxidant-triggered hemolysis.

question: A 32-year-old patient has morning dark urine, anemia, leukopenia, and an unprovoked hepatic vein thrombosis. Which molecular abnormality best unifies these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: A β-globin mutation can cause hemoglobinopathy but does not explain leukopenia with complement-sensitive cells.
A factor V mutation can cause thrombosis but does not produce hemolysis and leukopenia.
Spectrin mutations cause spherocytosis with extravascular destruction rather than pancytopenia and unusual thrombosis.
A prothrombin mutation promotes thrombosis but does not account for intravascular hemolysis or leukopenia.
An acquired PIGA mutation eliminates glycolipid-anchored protective proteins on multiple blood cell lines, causing complement-mediated hemolysis and thrombosis.

question: A patient has pallor, fatigue, and chronic gastrointestinal blood loss. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL [13.5-17.5 g/dL], MCV is 68 fL [80-100 fL], and the smear shows pale small erythrocytes. Which mechanism best explains the morphology?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.text: Reduced hemoglobin synthesis from iron depletion
options.rationale: Chronic blood loss depletes iron, limiting hemoglobin synthesis and producing microcytic hypochromic erythrocytes.

options.text: Increased hemoglobin loss through intravascular lysis
options.rationale: Intravascular hemolysis lowers haptoglobin and stimulates reticulocytosis rather than producing the stated chronic microcytic pattern.

options.text: Increased membrane loss during splenic passage
options.rationale: Membrane loss produces dense spherocytes without central pallor rather than pale microcytes.

options.text: Reduced precursor maturation from folate deficiency
options.rationale: Folate deficiency impairs nuclear maturation and produces megaloblastic macrocytosis.
Marrow replacement produces a leukoerythroblastic pattern rather than isolated hypochromic microcytosis.

question: A 65-year-old man has occult gastrointestinal bleeding, severe anemia, an MCV of 99 fL [80-100 fL], a reticulocyte percentage of 3.9% [0.5-2.5%], and marked erythroid hyperplasia. Which diagnosis best explains the near-normal MCV?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Aplastic anemia produces a hypocellular marrow with inadequate reticulocyte production.
Negative antiglobulin testing and chronic occult bleeding favor blood loss rather than antibody-mediated destruction.
Iron deficiency tends to lower MCV, while larger reticulocytes raise it, allowing the measured value to appear near normal.
Marrow replacement impairs sustained erythropoiesis and would produce a leukoerythroblastic smear.
Disseminated coagulation would produce coagulation-factor consumption and fragmented erythrocytes.

question: A patient has anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, fluctuating neurologic abnormalities, renal dysfunction, and fragmented erythrocytes. Which laboratory abnormality best supports the underlying diagnosis?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: This deficiency produces oxidant-associated hemolysis without the characteristic thrombocytopenic microvascular syndrome.
Spectrin defects cause spherocytes and extravascular destruction rather than fragmented cells and platelet consumption.
PIGA deficiency causes complement-sensitive pancytopenic cells and thrombosis rather than platelet-rich microthrombi.
ADAMTS13 deficiency permits very large von Willebrand factor multimers to drive platelet aggregation and microangiopathic hemolysis.
Reduced β-globin synthesis causes microcytic anemia with ineffective erythropoiesis rather than this pentad.

question: A 45-year-old woman has confusion, fever, petechiae, renal dysfunction, thrombocytopenia, and fragmented erythrocytes. Which molecular event most directly initiates the microvascular occlusions?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.text: Accumulation of large von Willebrand factor multimers
options.rationale: Failure to cleave very large von Willebrand factor multimers promotes widespread platelet aggregation in small vessels.

options.text: Accumulation of oxidized erythrocyte hemoglobin aggregates
options.rationale: Oxidized hemoglobin aggregates arise during oxidant injury and do not explain platelet-rich microthrombi.

options.text: Accumulation of unmatched globin chain precipitates
options.rationale: Unmatched globin chains damage erythroid precursors in thalassemia rather than causing acute platelet aggregation.

options.text: Accumulation of erythrocyte membrane cytoskeletal defects
options.rationale: Cytoskeletal abnormalities cause poorly deformable spherocytes and splenic sequestration.

options.text: Accumulation of activated plasma complement proteins
options.rationale: Complement activation lyses unprotected cells in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria rather than producing this pentad.

question: A child develops acute renal injury, thrombocytopenia, and fragmented erythrocytes after an episode of infectious gastroenteritis with diarrhea. Which process best distinguishes this disorder from thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: ADAMTS13 inhibition supports thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura rather than the postdiarrheal syndrome.
The postinfectious diarrheal setting supports toxin-mediated endothelial injury leading to hemolytic-uremic syndrome.
Complement-mediated lysis of unprotected blood cells would fit paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
Immune clearance produces a positive antiglobulin test and spherocytes rather than a diarrheal microangiopathy.
A cytoskeletal defect causes hereditary spherocytosis and does not explain acute renal failure after diarrhea.

question: A patient has thrombocytopenia and schistocytes after widespread activation and consumption of coagulation factors. Which diagnosis best fits this mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Review and integrate in a case-based format the fundamentals of macrocytic, normocytic, and microcytic anemia, and polycythemia by systematically evaluating and analyzing varying patient histories, symptoms, and laboratory findings

options.rationale: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura results from deficient cleavage of large von Willebrand factor multimers.
Hemolytic-uremic syndrome is associated with endothelial injury, commonly after infectious diarrhea.
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is associated with widespread thrombosis following heparin exposure.
Immune thrombocytopenic purpura primarily causes bleeding from isolated platelet loss without schistocytic hemolysis.
Disseminated intravascular coagulation consumes coagulation factors and platelets while generating microvascular erythrocyte fragmentation.
